component_findings.installers: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-4--typescript): Works wherever Node.js runs; version managers exist for all three major OS families (nvm for macOS/Linux, nvm-windows/Volta for Windows), though Windows requires a separate, community-maintained tool rather than the same script.
component_findings.package_version_manager: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-4--typescript): Primary channel is npm/yarn/pnpm; a secondary official channel exists via NuGet for MSBuild/Visual Studio projects, and editors (VS Code) bundle a built-in TypeScript language service version. OS-native package repositories often lag behind the latest compiler release, pushing users toward NodeSource or version managers for currency.

metric.installation_distribution_experie.limitations: Requires a Node.js runtime prerequisite before any TypeScript installation route works, which is an extra dependency step not present for some fully self-contained toolchains. | Global installs are explicitly discouraged by official docs in favor of project-local installs, meaning naive first-time global installs can drift from project-pinned versions if users don't follow best practice.
metric.installation_distribution_experie.selection_rule: Evaluate current official/de-facto installation paths on the same major desktop/server platforms and use only documented distribution channels.

metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.candidate_universe: Preserved candidate universe and findings from certified legacy work unit ecosystem-tooling--part-4--typescript; recertification did not select a new language-specific target.

component_findings.compat_deprecation: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-4--typescript): Breaking changes are intentionally front-loaded into the beta phase for early testing, showing process discipline, but this does not eliminate breaking changes at stable release boundaries; downstream projects (e.g. Backstage) build their own multi-month support-window policies on top of TypeScript's releases to manage this.
component_findings.governance_change: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-4--typescript): TypeScript publishes an explicit, well-documented release pipeline with predictable timing for beta, RC, stable, and patch stages.
component_findings.release_cadence: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-4--typescript): Maintenance/release cadence and documented stability commitments, including handling of major architecture transitions (0-25)
component_findings.release_integrity: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-4--typescript): TypeScript publishes an explicit, well-documented release pipeline with predictable timing for beta, RC, stable, and patch stages.
component_findings.support_policy: Preserved paid evidence (ecosystem-tooling--part-4--typescript): Versioning and support-policy clarity, including whether version numbers reliably signal breaking vs. non-breaking changes (0-25)

metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.limitations: Non-semver versioning is a structural, long-standing characteristic (not a one-time event) that reduces the reliability of version numbers as a stability signal for all consumers, including enterprise adopters who build their own external support-window policies to compensate. | The ongoing Go-native compiler transition (TS 7.0 GA July 2026, full programmatic API deferred to 7.1) is a major, currently incomplete architectural change; it was scored as observable current evidence per the frozen rubric, not as a bonus/penalty for language age.
metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.selection_rule: Score current observable release/support practices. Language age and first-release date are context only and never directly score.
